title: Maybe the Rapture is already here
gist: Noah Smith argues that mass culture and meme culture have been replaced by AI-curated vertical short-form video, which turns social media into passive, isolating entertainment akin to 'heavenbanning'; he links smartphones to collapsing fertility via fewer couples forming, citing studies showing iPhone and 3G access reduced births.

themes.theme: Collapse of mass and meme culture

insights.claim: 76 million people watched Seinfeld's finale in 1998 versus fewer than 20 million for Game of Thrones' finale two decades later, and there is no longer any show that everyone watches.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Fragmented audiences erode the value of mass-reach media and advertising inventory.
insights.quote: 76 million people watched the last episode of Seinfeld in 1998; fewer than 20 million watched the last episode of Game of Thrones two decades later.
insights.locator: The mass culture of my youth

insights.claim: The 2010s meme culture driven by Twitter and Facebook feeds has largely disappeared, and X persists but is diminished in scope and relevance, at times feeling like a ghost town.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Text-based social platforms are losing cultural centrality and engagement share.
insights.quote: Twitter — now X — has not died but is diminished in scope and relevance.
insights.locator: There are almost no memes left

insights.claim: The internet has converged ('carcinized') on a single format, the vertically scrolling short-video feed, invented by Vine, popularized by TikTok and copied by every other site.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Platforms without competitive short-form feeds face share loss in attention.
insights.quote: the entire internet has steadily carcinized into a single type of app/website/media/entertainment — a vertically scrolling feed full of short video clips
insights.locator: But my bet is that they’re just watching

insights.claim: Per Ampere data, vertical short-form video feeds are now more dominant than every form of media except social media itself.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Ad budgets and creator economics are shifting toward short-form video platforms.

insights.claim: Data cited from John Burn-Murdoch show 'social media' has shifted from people messaging and posting to each other toward mostly passive video watching, with even YouTube increasingly showing short clips.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Social platforms are becoming entertainment/TV substitutes, changing competitive sets and ad models.
insights.quote: This shift has basically killed the original use of social media, turning it from a town square or conversation room into a form of purely passive entertainment

insights.claim: Smith predicts that much short-form feed content will soon be AI-generated and, as compute costs fall, personalized for each user to maximize engagement and in-app purchases rather than delight.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Generative video could slash content costs for platforms and boost monetization while displacing human creators.
insights.quote: as the cost of compute drops, AI will be able to generate personalized videos for everyone
insights.locator: Right now, short-form videos are mostly

insights.claim: AI-curated short-form feeds function like 'heavenbanning', isolating users in personalized content that people they know never see.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rising isolation may carry regulatory and social backlash risk for feed-based platforms.
insights.quote: It’s possible to think of vertical short-form video feeds as a kind of heavenbanning.
insights.locator: It’s possible to think of vertical

insights.claim: A study of more than 1,500 Chinese high-school students found a steady diet of short-form videos damaged their future time perspective, making them less able to plan for the future.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Evidence of cognitive harm strengthens the case for youth social media regulation.
insights.quote: in a study involving more than 1,500 high-school students, found that their future time perspective was damaged by a steady diet of such short-form videos
insights.locator: Researchers at several universities in China

insights.claim: Fertility decline is increasingly driven by people never forming couples rather than couples choosing fewer children, with social media's isolating effects an obvious culprit.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Demographic decline is accelerating, with long-run implications for labor supply, growth and pensions.
insights.quote: now, it’s increasingly about people never forming couples at all

insights.claim: Myers and Hooper (2026) found access to the iPhone reduced births by 4.5-8.0% at ages 15-19 and 3.2-6.6% at ages 20-24.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Quantifies a technology-driven drag on birth rates.
insights.quote: access to the iPhone reduced births by 4.5–8.0% at ages 15–19 and 3.2–6.6% at ages 20–24

insights.claim: Breen et al. (2026) found 3G coverage expansion in Nigeria reduced the annual probability of a woman giving birth by 7%.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Smartphone-driven fertility decline may spread to emerging markets as connectivity grows, reshaping their demographic dividend.
insights.quote: the expansion of 3G coverage [in Nigeria] during the study period led to a decline in fertility, corresponding to a 7% reduction in the annual probability of a woman having a birth.

insights.claim: Smith argues smartphones are the likeliest explanation for rich- and middle-income-country fertility falling through the ~2 floor toward zero, and help explain why Latin America now has lower birth rates than the EU.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Middle-income demographic decline undermines growth assumptions for emerging markets like Latin America.
insights.quote: Smartphones at least help to explain why Latin America now has an even lower birth rate than the EU.
insights.locator: Given the timing and the microeconomic evidence

insights.claim: Smith speculates that AI-personalized short-form content could be a 'Great Filter' that lets a species hack its reward function and dwindle away rather than expand.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the attention economy as a potential long-run existential demographic risk.
insights.locator: I think about the Great Filter sometimes
